title: Relational operators: comparing values

visuals.title: Compare a and b: slide the numbers and see which comparisons hold

branches.label: a equals b: so a == b, a >= b and a <= b are true (1). a != b, a > b and a < b are false (0).
a is greater than b: so a > b, a >= b and a != b are true (1). The others are false (0).

visuals.elseLabel: a is less than b: so a < b, a <= b and a != b are true (1). The others are false (0).

visuals.title: Match each operator to its meaning

pairs.meaning: Is greater than or equal to
Is less than or equal to
Assignment: stores a value in a variable (does NOT compare)

goal: After this you can compare two values with ==, !=, >, <, >= and <=, read the true/false (1/0) result, and never mix up = with ==.
warmup: In daily life we compare all the time. Is my mobile balance more than Rs. 100? Is the rickshaw fare equal to the money in my pocket? Is my exam mark at least 50? Every one of these questions has only two possible answers: yes or no. A program asks the same kind of question, and the answer is true or false.
definition: A relational operator compares two values. The result is a Boolean value: true or false. C++ prints true as 1 and false as 0. The type that stores such a value is called bool. Example: with a = 10 and b = 20, the expression a < b is true, so it gives 1.
howItWorks: Move the sliders. The computer looks at a and b, then tests each operator. Exactly one of three things is always true: a is less than b, a equals b, or a is greater than b. The six operators are just different ways to ask about these three cases. In the next lessons the if statement uses this true/false answer to decide what to do.
syntax:
a == b    // equal to              (true if both values are the same)
a != b    // not equal to          (true if the values are different)
a > b     // greater than
a < b     // less than
a >= b    // greater than or equal to   (> first, then =)
a <= b    // less than or equal to

bool ok = (a < b);   // a bool variable stores true (1) or false (0)
cout << (a < b);     // prints 1 or 0; keep the brackets around the comparison

// Careful: = stores a value, == compares two values

sample.title: Printing comparison results

explanation.text: a is a whole-number variable that holds 10.
10 is not equal to 20, so the answer is false and C++ prints 0. The brackets keep the comparison together.
10 and 20 are different, so the answer is true and C++ prints 1.
10 is greater than or equal to 10 (it is equal): true, prints 1.

steps.note: The program starts at main().
a is created and holds 10.
b is created and holds 20.
Is 10 equal to 20? No, so the result is false. cout prints 0.
Is 10 different from 20? Yes, so the result is true. cout prints 1.
Is 10 less than 20? Yes: true, prints 1.
Is 10 at least 10? Yes (it is equal): true, prints 1.
The program ends.

sample.title: Storing a comparison in a bool
sample.expectedOutput: Enter budget and price: Can buy (1 = yes, 0 = no): 1

explanation.text: Two whole-number variables: the money you have and the price.
Reads the two numbers typed by the user (separated by a space).
Compares budget with price. The answer (true or false) is stored in a bool variable called canBuy.
Prints the message and then canBuy. A bool prints as 1 (true) or 0 (false).

steps.note: The program starts.
budget and price are created (no value yet).
The prompt is shown.
The user typed 500 and 450, so budget = 500 and price = 450.
Is 500 >= 450? Yes, so canBuy becomes true (1).
Prints the message and the value of canBuy.
The program ends.

worked.problem: What is the output of the following program? (An exam favourite: = versus ==.)
pseudocode: PRINT (x = 5): this STORES 5 in x, and its value is 5
worked.flowchartMermaid:
flowchart TD
  A([Start]) --> B[x = 3]
  B --> C[/Print x == 5/]
  C --> D["Assign x = 5 and print it"]
  D --> E[/Print x == 5/]
  E --> F[/Print x/]
  F --> G([End])

sample.title: The = versus == trap

explanation.text: Comparison only: 3 is not 5, so it prints 0. x does not change.
A single = is assignment. It stores 5 in x, and the value of the whole expression is 5, so 5 is printed.
Now x is 5, so the comparison is true and 1 is printed.

steps.note: The program starts.
x is created with value 3.
Compare 3 with 5: false. Prints 0. x stays 3.
Single = assigns: x becomes 5. The value of the expression is 5, so 5 is printed.
Now x is 5, so 5 == 5 is true. Prints 1.
Prints the current value of x.
The program ends.

Check if two values are different
Strictly greater / strictly less (equal does not count)
Greater or equal / less or equal (equal counts)
Keep a true/false answer in a variable for later

mistakes.error: expected primary-expression before '>' token (the > must come first: >=)
no match for 'operator>' (cout << a is evaluated first, so use brackets)
usually compiles with no error, which makes it dangerous: it stores 5 in x and is always true
lvalue required as left operand of assignment

examTips: Remember: true prints as 1 and false prints as 0.
= stores a value. == compares. Examiners love this trap.
>= and <= count equal values as true; > and < do not.
Write the two symbols in the right order: >= and <=, never => or =<.
Put brackets around a comparison inside cout: cout << (a > b);
romanSummary: Relational operators do values ko compare karte hain aur true (1) ya false (0) dete hain.
Ek = value store karta hai, aur do == compare karte hain. Ye sab se bari ghalti hai.
True aur false ko bool variable mein bhi rakh sakte hain.

practice.prompt: What is the value of the expression 7 != 7?
practice.explanation: 7 is the same as 7, so 'not equal' is false, which prints as 0.

practice.prompt: Fill in the blank: the operator that means 'not equal to' is ______.
practice.hint: It is made of an exclamation mark and an equals sign.
practice.explanation: != is true when the two values are different.

practice.hint: Each comparison prints one digit, with no space between them.
practice.explanation: 8 > 5 is true (1), 8 < 5 is false (0), 8 == 8 is true (1). Output: 101.

practice.prompt:
Fix the bug so that it prints 1 when marks is at least 50:

cout << (marks => 50);
practice.hint: The two symbols are in the wrong order.
practice.explanation: The correct operator is >= (greater than first, then equals).

practice.hint: Work out the arithmetic first, then compare.
practice.explanation: a + b is 13 and 13 > 12 is true. a * 2 is 8 and b - 1 is 8, so they are equal: true. 4 <= 9 is true. Output: 111.

practice.explanation: (x = 0) stores 0 in x and its value is 0, so 0 is printed. Then x == 0 is true, so 1 is printed.

practice.explanation: a == b gives true (1) or false (0), and cout prints that number.

quiz.hint: One symbol stores, two symbols compare.
5 is bigger than 3, so the comparison is true.

quiz.prompt: Which expression is true when marks is 50?
quiz.hint: Equal values count only for >= and <=.
quiz.explanation: marks > 50 is false when marks is 50, but marks >= 50 is true.

options: Stores 5 in x and is always true
quiz.answer: Stores 5 in x and is always true
